summary: This experimental document specifies how DTLS can protect RADIUS traffic. Plain RADIUS has limited authentication and encryption and depends on fixed shared secrets, so using DTLS gives stronger security.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC carries RADIUS packets inside DTLS, while keeping the RADIUS packet format. DTLS adds encryption and peer authentication, but it does not add reliable or in-order delivery.

questions: what port does radius dtls use
subtitle: Encapsulating unchanged RADIUS packets in DTLS to add transport security over UDP.

tldr.problem: RADIUS over UDP sends packet data in the clear, uses MD5-based checks and fixed shared secrets, and does not prevent verbatim replay of packets.
tldr.mechanism: The client passes each RADIUS packet to DTLS over UDP. The server tracks sessions by source and destination IP addresses and ports and applies rules for authentication, timeouts and closure.
tldr.outcome: RADIUS/DTLS is Experimental and was updated by RFC 9765. The RFC does not recommend long-term RADIUS/UDP use outside isolated and secure networks.

today: RFC 7360 is an Experimental RFC and was updated by RFC 9765. It advises against long-term RADIUS/UDP use outside isolated and secure networks.

sections.title: Why Protect RADIUS with DTLS
sections.content:
Traditional RADIUS uses MD5-based methods for per-packet authentication and integrity, and its traffic can be sent in the clear. The RFC describes risks including replay of packets and dependence on fixed shared secrets. IPsec can protect RADIUS traffic, but its security policy is part of network configuration and is not directly controlled by the RADIUS application.

This specification uses Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) as the RADIUS transport. RADIUS remains UDP-based, and the application can monitor and control the associated security policy. DTLS does not provide reliable or in-order delivery and does not fragment application messages.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects RADIUS traffic while keeping RADIUS on UDP. It does not make delivery reliable or put packets in order.

sections.title: What Changes in the Transport
sections.content:
The RADIUS packet format, permitted codes, authenticators, attributes and other packet calculations remain unchanged. A RADIUS application creates its packet as usual and gives it to DTLS instead of sending it directly through a UDP socket. Implementations MUST support encapsulated RADIUS packets of 4096 octets.

Two details change: length checks use the decrypted DTLS data length, and extra decrypted octets beyond the RADIUS Length field are treated as padding. The shared secret used for RADIUS's MD5 integrity checks and attribute encryption is the fixed string radius/dtls.
sections.plainLanguage: The RADIUS message stays the same; DTLS carries it as the transport. The receiver checks the RADIUS length against decrypted DTLS data, not the UDP packet length.

sections.title: Ports and Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
The default destination is UDP port 2083. All packets received there MUST be treated as DTLS, and servers MUST NOT accept RADIUS/UDP on that port or accept DTLS on the older RADIUS/UDP ports. Clients and servers need administrator configuration because RADIUS has no protocol negotiation.

A client configured for DTLS MUST NOT fall back to RADIUS/UDP if the server appears unresponsive. Both sides must authenticate their peers. Allowing one client to use both RADIUS/UDP and RADIUS/DTLS is not recommended because it can expose traffic to a downgrade attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators choose DTLS in advance because RADIUS cannot negotiate the transport. A client configured for DTLS must treat an unresponsive server as down, not switch to RADIUS/UDP.

sections.title: Tracking and Closing DTLS Sessions
sections.content:
Because UDP does not track sessions, a server records each DTLS session using the source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port. When it needs to retransmit a RADIUS response, it caches the RADIUS response and sends it through DTLS again; it must not retransmit an old DTLS packet.

Servers should use DTLS cookies to reduce denial-of-service risk from forged UDP traffic and must limit partially open sessions. Sessions are deleted after closure alerts, malformed packets or failed authentication checks. Idle sessions should be removed after a configurable timeout between 60 and 600 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tracks a session using the two IP addresses and two ports. It closes sessions that fail security checks and removes sessions that stay idle beyond the configured timeout.

sections.title: Credentials and Remaining Risks
sections.content:
DTLS mitigates many RADIUS encryption and authorization weaknesses, but the unchanged RADIUS packet format still has its own considerations. The fixed secret radius/dtls is acceptable only with non-null encryption. A RADIUS/UDP shared secret MUST NOT be reused for DTLS or converted into a TLS pre-shared key.

Each peer must authenticate the other using TLS credentials. The RFC recommends that clients begin with an empty list of trusted certificate authorities and add authorities through administrator configuration. Pre-shared keys must be at least 16 octets; the RFC recommends generating them with a cryptographically secure random-number generator.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS credentials must be separate from the old RADIUS/UDP shared secret. Clients should trust only certificate authorities selected by an administrator.
